title: To Call or Not to Call: Diagnosing Intrinsic Over-Calling Bias in LLM Agents
claim: Agents call tools even when unneeded because of an activation-independent bias, which a calibrated counter-shift can cancel.
layout: 3 panels: large left data panel, right column with conceptual plot above AMCS flow
description: The figure has three panels. Panel (a), the largest, fills the left and is titled "Over-calling in Tool use decisions". It holds two sub-panels. On the left, paired bar charts show call, overall and no-call accuracy for three model families, each with a larger model (solid bars) and a smaller one (hatched bars). Call accuracy is high, at 90–99%. No-call accuracy is much lower, at 2–44%. On the right is "A typical failure": a stacked dialogue with a system prompt, a user request ("Play a song on Spotify"), missing-information bubbles (song name? device ID?), a red hallucinated-call output, and a green correct behavior of asking for information. Panel (b) is a sigmoid curve of P(call) against activation margin m, with the neutral boundary m* left of parity at m=0. Panel (c) is a small flow, diagnosed bias to counter-bias shift to fewer false calls, with base and AMCS bar comparisons.
caption: Overview of over-calling, intrinsic bias, and AMCS. (a) Across six target models, call accuracy is high, but no-call accuracy is much lower, reducing overall accuracy; a representative case shows the model calling a tool despite missing required information. (b) Intrinsic Bias Hypothesis: at activation parity (m = 0), the decision still favors CALL; the neutral boundary shifts to m⋆< 0. (c) AMCS converts the diagnosed bias β0 into a counter-bias shift δ, aiming to reduce false calls while preserving valid calls.
abstract: LLM agents exhibit a consistent tendency to over-call, invoking tools even in situations where none is needed. On the When2Call benchmark, six models from three families show high call accuracy but much lower no-call accuracy, leaving overall accuracy in the 55%-70% range. We trace this to an Intrinsic Bias Hypothesis (IBH): the call/no-call decision mapping carries an activation-independent call offset, so the model favors call even at activation parity. Using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), we recover behavior-aligned feature bases for the call/no_call decision, reduce them to a signed activation margin, and estimate the offset directly. Across all six models, the model is decision-neutral only when no_call activation outweighs call activation, consistent with IBH. We then causally test IBH with Adaptive Margin-Calibrated Steering (AMCS), a closed-form counter-bias shift along SAE decoder directions. Cancelling the diagnosed offset mitigates over-calling and improves overall accuracy with a negligible drop in call accuracy. Our work recasts over-calling from an empirical phenomenon into a mechanistic object amenable to causal correction. Code is available at https://github.com/SKURA502/agent-sae/.
